analysis.one_liner: Requires cruise ships to report crimes, install security cameras and trained medical staff, and expands families' right to sue for deaths at sea.
analysis.headline: A bipartisan bill with 17 cosponsors (15 Democrats, 2 Republicans) never received a committee hearing or a vote and died when the 111th Congress ended in January 2011; most of its security requirements passed in similar form in a 2010 law.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have required cruise ships serving U.S. ports to log and report serious crimes to the FBI and Coast Guard, post public crime data online by cruise line name, install peep holes, latches, cameras and overboard detection, restrict crew access to passenger rooms, keep rape kits and a trained doctor aboard, and certify crew in evidence collection. It would also have let Coast Guard personnel serve as public safety officers aboard ships and extended families' right to sue for wrongful death at sea from 3 to 12 miles from shore, including compensation for loss of companionship.
analysis.who_benefits: Cruise passengers, crewmembers who are victims of crime, and the families of people who die or disappear at sea. The bill's findings note about 12 million passengers a year, that sexual and physical assaults were the leading crimes reported to the FBI involving cruise ships, and that victims often do not know their rights or whom to contact after an attack.

how_it_helps.text: Requires masters to report homicides, suspicious deaths, missing U.S. nationals, kidnappings, serious assaults, and sexual offenses to the FBI and Coast Guard, closing a gap where no federal rule required cruise lines to report crimes outside U.S. territorial waters.
Mandates the Coast Guard publish a public website, updated quarterly and broken out by cruise line name, counting missing persons and alleged crimes, and requires each cruise line to link to it.

Requires ships to carry rape kits, anti-retroviral medication, a U.S.-licensed doctor trained in forensic sexual assault exams, confidential hotline access, and to keep medical findings from the cruise line without the victim's written consent.

Requires ship design retrofits (higher rails, peep holes, security latches, cameras, overboard detection) and certified crime-scene evidence training for crew, with annual Coast Guard inspections and denial of U.S. entry for violators.

Extends wrongful-death jurisdiction from 3 to 12 nautical miles and allows families to recover nonpecuniary damages — loss of care, comfort, and companionship, and the decedent's pre-death pain and suffering.

analysis.who_pays: Cruise lines, most of them foreign-flagged, would bear the retrofit, staffing, training, inspection, and reporting costs, plus expanded lawsuit liability for deaths near U.S. shores; those costs could feed into ticket prices.

drawbacks.text: Compliance is costly: a U.S.-licensed forensic-trained doctor aboard every ship, retrofits across an entire fleet, and certified security staff on every voyage, costs that foreign-flagged operators argue would raise fares for the very passengers the bill protects.

The bill's own findings concede enforcement is tangled: most ships calling at U.S. ports fly foreign flags, and crimes at sea can involve multiple countries' jurisdiction, making the reporting and liability rules harder to apply in practice.

Expanding the Death on the High Seas Act to nonpecuniary damages would increase litigation exposure for operators and their insurers, a change the industry fought hard even as it accepted the safety equipment mandates in the version enacted later.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The safety and reporting requirements address a real, documented problem — unreported sexual assaults and disappearances with no law enforcement aboard — and the direct costs are modest relative to a 2,000-passenger, 950-crew vessel's operations. The genuinely contentious part is the liability expansion, which shifts money to victims' families and their lawyers; a fair reading is that the security provisions were worth their cost, while the wrongful-death damages change was the industry's strongest honest objection.

outcome.mechanism: The House referred the bill to the Transportation and Infrastructure Committee, which passed it to its Coast Guard subcommittee, where it sat with no hearing, no markup, and no vote until the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Doris Matsui introduced the bill on March 12, 2009 with bipartisan original cosponsors, including Rep. Ted Poe of Texas.
It was referred the same day to the House Committee on Transportation and Infrastructure and the next day to the Subcommittee on Coast Guard and Maritime Transportation.
The action history shows no further action — no hearing, no markup, no floor vote — before the 111th Congress ended on January 3, 2011.
The bill attracted 17 cosponsors, 15 Democrats and 2 Republicans.

A substantially similar Cruise Vessel Security and Safety Act did become law in 2010 as part of the Coast Guard Authorization Act, but the version enacted left out this bill's expansion of wrongful-death damages, which the cruise industry had opposed.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Cruise lines came out ahead in the short run: they avoided the compliance costs, public per-line crime data, and the wrongful-death liability expansion. Passengers did not get the protections from this bill, though most of the security requirements became law in 2010 anyway; the damages expansion did not.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Cruise lines avoided the costs, for now

for.name: Doris Matsui
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and recruited bipartisan cosponsors.

for.name: Ted Poe
for.what_they_did: Joined as an original cosponsor at introduction.

against.name: House Transportation and Infrastructure Committee

sides.party_line_note: Cosponsorship was bipartisan but small — 15 of 253 House Democrats and 2 of 178 House Republicans — and no vote was ever taken, so no roll-call split exists.

industries.industry: Cruise lines (mostly foreign-flagged operators such as Carnival and Royal Caribbean)
industries.note: The bill would impose retrofit, medical staffing, reporting, and inspection costs, publish crime data by company name, and let families sue for wrongful death out to 12 miles with nonpecuniary damages. The industry's interest — avoiding those costs and lawsuits — ran directly against the safety interests of the roughly 12 million passengers a year the bill cited, and the industry's opposition outlasted this bill: the 2010 law adopted the security mandates but dropped the damages expansion.

industries.industry: Maritime security and medical equipment suppliers
industries.note: Mandated peep holes, security latches, video surveillance, overboard detection, acoustic hailing devices, and rape kits would create demand for their products.
